football_evidence.question: Can Virginia get Wake Forest off the field on third down?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Wake Forest, and its own breakdown accounts for about 1.0 of the 5.0 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Wake Forest has the ball (big plays through the air): Wake Forest’s offense turns 14.4% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Virginia’s defense gives up explosive gains on 10.4% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.3%).

When Virginia has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Virginia’s offense has allowed a sack on 11.3% of its dropbacks, and Wake Forest’s defense sacks the quarterback on 5.4% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).

When Virginia has the ball (big plays through the air): Virginia’s offense turns 9.4% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Wake Forest’s defense gives up explosive gains on 5.1% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.3%).

When Virginia has the ball (big plays on the ground): Virginia’s offense turns 5.2% of its runs into explosive gains, and Wake Forest’s defense gives up explosive gains on 2.7% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.5%).
contradicting: Eli Holstein has completed 12 of 18 passes (66.7%) for 180 yards, 10.0 yards per attempt, 3 touchdowns and no interceptions in two games for Virginia, and has been sacked on 2 of 20 dropbacks.
EdgeDesk’s position-group ratings put Virginia’s running backs No. 35 nationally and Wake Forest’s No. 122.

Beau Pribula has completed 119 of 187 passes (63.6%) for 1,419 yards, 7.6 yards per attempt, 13 touchdowns and 2 interceptions in eight games for Virginia, and has been sacked on 24 of 211 dropbacks.
